## In one sentence

Probability models describe uncertainty, distributions describe random
quantities, and sampling connects a population to the data we observe.

## Distributions

A distribution describes which values are plausible and how common they are. A
probability mass function is used for discrete outcomes; a density describes
continuous outcomes. The mean gives a centre and the variance gives spread, but
shape, tails, and dependence also matter.

The normal distribution is often useful as an approximation, not a universal law.
The central limit theorem says that suitably scaled averages can become
approximately normal under broad conditions as sample size grows.

## Sampling

A population is the target set; a sample is the observed subset. Random sampling
supports generalisation when the sampling frame represents the target. A
convenience sample can be precise about itself while still being biased for the
population of interest.

::: {.callout-important}
Independence is a modelling assumption, not a synonym for "different rows." Time
series, clusters, families, and repeated measurements often contain dependence.
:::
